chapter: England, later career and closing thoughts
title: Jazz versus rock and roll, and her first airplane flight
summary: Jazz takes years of work unlike quick rock success, and she describes her first flight to Sacramento last May.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Now, I don't know, I guess the rock and roll scene has made quite an impact too, but somehow it hasn't lasted. It's not a lasting thing, unfortunately. Somebody makes money real fast, real quick and fast, you know. But the thing with

the jazz artists is that you knock yourself out a long time before you can even learn to play an instrument. You don't do this overnight, you know. And of course with the new electronic gimmicks and the instruments and all the things that's going on today, it has made it a faster thing. It's just like flying, for instance, and the train, you know. I just took my first flight last -- when was it, May? And I tried to -- I have it written down someplace. I think it was -- I went to San Francisco. I was en route to Sacramento, and I was a special guest at the Sacramento Jazz Club. I was their surprise guest at their 10th anniversary, so they wanted me to be their guest, and I flew. But I'm saying all that to say it was just like that, because that was my first time flying, and they had a heck of a time getting me on the plane then. But flying is something I just don't -- it hasn't really gotten to me yet, however I realize in some instances it is a necessity. But if I was travelling all the time I still couldn't -- I couldn't stand the, you know, the tension, the thing of flying. I don't think I could stand that. Well, I was spoiled, I guess, coming along in the era of the train bit, you know, before anybody even heard of the word Amtrak.
